messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Leilani had been a police officer for forty-two years, long enough to believe she had seen the worst of what people could do to one another. But nothing in her long career prepared her for the moment her own world shattered on a sunny Tuesday afternoon. She was driving her grandson, Manu, home from his summer job, lecturing him gently about saving money for college. In the split second she turned her head to emphasize a point, a pickup truck ran the red light. For Leilani, the memory isn't a story she tells but a series of brutal, sensory fragments that ambush her. It comes most often as a set of still pictures, as vivid and sharp as a crime scene photograph: the blue of the other truck just before impact, the web of cracks spreading across the passenger-side window, the impossible angle of Manu’s head against the headrest. When these images strike, she sometimes hears the sound again, a deafening, metallic scream that drowns out everything else, the same sound she heard in the moments before the silence that followed.

In the eight months since the accident, Leilani has constructed her life around avoiding these fragments. At the precinct, where she now works a desk assignment, talk of traffic incidents has become unbearable. When a younger officer begins recounting a DUI arrest, Leilani will abruptly get up to refill her coffee or busy herself with filing, her heart hammering against her ribs. She feels their eyes on her, knows they are aware of what happened to Manu, and she is certain they are judging her. The deepest conviction she holds is that the accident was her fault. "I was looking at him," she told her husband, Mateo, once in the dead of night. "I was lecturing him. I took my eyes off the road." This belief has settled into her bones, a cold, heavy certainty that she, a protector by trade, had failed in the most fundamental way. She should have protected him, and she hadn't.

The triggers are everywhere. The smell of alcohol, once just a background note in her line of work, is now a direct threat. When Mateo opened a beer a few weeks ago while watching a football game, the scent of hops and yeast hit her from across the room, and she was instantly back in the wreckage, smelling the spilled cans from the other driver's truck. She fled to the bedroom, unable to explain the wave of nausea and terror. Her avoidance has carved new, inconvenient paths into her life. She now takes a twenty-minute detour to work to avoid the intersection where the crash occurred. Seeing any roadside accident, even a minor fender-bender, can hijack her entire day, leaving her shaky and disoriented, the vivid image of her own crumpled car superimposed over the scene. This sense of ambient threat has solidified into a bleak worldview; she feels utterly powerless, convinced that catastrophic events are random and unstoppable, and that her decades of service, of imposing order on chaos, were a foolish illusion.

The consequence of this new reality has been a slow, painful withdrawal from the family she fought so hard to protect. Manu is recovering, slowly, but Leilani finds it hard to be around him. His physical therapy milestones feel like accusations. His laughter sounds like a prelude to more pain. The breaking point came last week, when Manu, with his parents’ blessing, started talking about getting his driver’s license reinstated. The thought of him behind the wheel of a car filled Leilani not with pride, but with a suffocating dread. She realized then that her fear was building a wall between her and her grandson, and that the guilt she carried was poisoning the very love that was supposed to be his comfort. She came to therapy because the memories are not fading; they are as clear as the day they were forged. She is terrified that she has been permanently broken by the event, but a small part of her hopes to one day be able to sit in a car beside her grandson and see not a future catastrophe, but simply the young man she loves.
